nodes.description: Within infected fetal tissues (developing lens, retina, cochlear organ of Corti, cardiac outflow tract, and brain), rubella virus capsid protein binds host protein p32, disrupting mitochondrial distribution and morphology, inducing apoptosis, and inhibiting cell population proliferation. In the developing brain, rubella virus infects microglia within heterogeneous neural environments and provokes a profound interferon response in surrounding neurons and neural progenitor cells. This arrest of organogenesis produces the classical Gregg triad of congenital cataracts (along with pigmentary retinopathy), sensorineural deafness, and congenital heart defects as well as microcephaly and intellectual disability.

evidence.snippet: We show that in human brain slices, rubella virus predominantly infects microglia. This infection occurs in a heterogeneous population but not in a highly microglia-enriched monoculture in the absence of other cell types. By using an organoid-microglia model, we further demonstrate that rubella virus infection leads to a profound interferon response in non-microglial cells, including neurons and neural progenitor cells

evidence.reference_title: Rubella virus infection in endothelial cells reduces angiogenesis via interferon betainduced CXCL10
evidence.snippet: Endothelial cells (EC) of the placenta are infected by rubella virus (RuV). RuV reduced angiogenic and migratory capacity of primary human EC whereas cell cycle and apoptosis rate were not affected. Next generation sequencing analysis revealed an induction of antiviral type I and III interferons (IFN) that induced angiogenesis-inhibiting cytokines such as CXCL10.

evidence.reference_title: Delayed manifestations of congenital rubella.
evidence.snippet: Several mechanisms of pathogenesis of the damage have to be considered for the delayed manifestations, including growth of the virus in tissues, resulting in a reduced growth rate and shortened life-span of the cells; autoimmune responses, initially stimulated by the infection; genetic susceptibility; vascular damage by the viral infection with further stenosis or occlusion of the vessels later; reactive hypervascularization; and chronic persistence of the virus in the tissue with subsequent extension of the infection to other areas.
